title: How Two Men and a Map Split Korea: The 38th Parallel From Both Sides
sources: National Interest, 'How 2 Colonels and a National Geographic Map Divided Korea': https://nationalinterest.org/node/10222 (evening of 10 Aug 1945, an office in the Pentagon, Rusk and Bonesteel, the National Geographic map without provincial borders, Rusk's 'Neither Tic nor I was a Korea expert' and 'Seoul, the capital, should be in the American sector')

beats.date:
FRIDAY, 10 AUGUST 1945
THE PENTAGON · WASHINGTON, D.C.
beats.say: Friday, the tenth of August, 1945. Washington, late in the evening.
Japan has just offered to surrender. The war is almost over... and nobody has decided what happens to Korea.
Inside the Pentagon, two colonels step into a quiet room next door.
Dean Rusk. And Charles Bonesteel. Neither of them is an expert on Korea.
On the desk is a National Geographic map of Asia. It doesn't even show Korea's provinces.
They know one thing. Seoul, the capital, should be on the American side.
So a red pencil goes across the map... just north of Seoul. The thirty-eighth parallel.
Seven thousand miles away, it is already Saturday in Korea. Twenty-five million people are going about their day.
Not one of them knows... that their country has just been cut in two.
Here is what the line will cost. Within five years, Korea will fight a war that kills about a million soldiers, and between one and a half and three million civilians.
On the way, we will meet the officers who drew the line, the dictator who accepted it, an exile who wanted a country, and a young guerrilla who became a ruler.
This is how Korea was split, in 1945: the 38th parallel, the United States, the Soviet Union, and the Koreans caught between them.
It is the story of two men and a map. And it asks a hard question. Was the line an accident, or did the Cold War make it permanent?
To understand the line, start with what was there before it. For more than a thousand years, Korea had been one country. Then, in 1910, Japan annexed it.
Five years earlier, Korea had become a protectorate of Japan. The emperor, Gojong, was deposed. For thirty-five years, Koreans lived under foreign rule in their own land.
Koreans fought back, but they never spoke with one voice. Nationalists and radicals split over methods and goals. And a government in exile, the Korean Provisional Government, worked from China.
In 1919, Koreans protested Japanese rule in the March First Movement. Japan crushed it. After that, many activists left. Syngman Rhee joined the government in exile, in Shanghai.
It struggled for years to get anyone to recognize it. That mattered later. When the empire fell, there was no single Korean authority ready to take over.
Meanwhile, the great powers were already talking about Korea. In November 1943, Roosevelt, Churchill and Chiang Kai-shek met in Cairo.
They promised that, quote, in due course Korea shall become free and independent. Notice the words. In due course.
Remember this feeling. In 1945, Koreans did not want a new master. They wanted their country back, whole, and in their own hands.
Roosevelt had a plan for that wait. A trusteeship, run by the great powers, until Koreans were ready to govern themselves. He raised it with Stalin. Stalin did not disagree.
So for Koreans, the end of the war was not a clean break. It was a handover, and every great power had a plan for it, except the people who lived there.
It sounded sensible in a conference room. To Koreans, who had waited thirty-five years, it sounded like one more landlord.
Now jump to August 1945. On the sixth, the first atomic bomb falls on Hiroshima. Two days later, the Soviet Union declares war on Japan.
Stalin had promised his allies he would join the Pacific war. Now he does, with a huge army, right next to Korea.
A Soviet commander calls on Koreans to rise against Japan. His words: a banner of liberty and independence is rising in Seoul.
On the tenth of August, Soviet troops cross into northern Korea. They meet little resistance, and they are moving fast.
Soviet ships and troops land in the northeast within days. On the sixteenth, they land at Wonsan. By the twenty-fourth, they hold most of the major cities in the north.
In Washington, officials grow anxious. If the Red Army keeps going, it could take all of Korea before a single American soldier lands.
Someone has to draw a line, fast. And that is how two young officers, Dean Rusk and Charles Bonesteel, end up in a room with a map.

Meet the first. Dean Rusk, thirty-six years old, a colonel. He was born to a poor cotton-farming family in rural Georgia. He worked his way through a small Presbyterian college, and won a Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford.

Meet the second. Charles Bonesteel, thirty-five. His classmates at West Point called him Tick. His father was a major general, and his grandfather an army major. And he, too, had been a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford.
Two Rhodes scholars, one deadline. With a general named George Lincoln, they were drafting the surrender order for Japan. The document that would tell each army where to accept the surrender.
Neither of them was a Korea specialist. Rusk would later admit he did not know Korean history. Tonight, that did not matter. All they needed was a line.
Think how fast this is. A war ends. A line is drawn. An army moves. And ordinary Koreans, who have not been told anything, are left to guess what is happening to their country.
It is the tenth of August as well. They have been told to define an American zone. They have extremely short notice, and they are completely unprepared.
But the plan assumed the Soviets would stop where they were told. Nobody could be sure. And the next decision would be made very quickly.
The map is from the National Geographic. No Korea expert is asked. The Koreans are not consulted.

chapters.title: A Line on a Magazine Map

beats.say: They look for a line that does two things. First, it should cut the country roughly in half. Second, it must put Seoul, the capital, on the American side.
The thirty-eighth parallel does both. It runs just north of Seoul, and it splits the peninsula nearly down the middle.
Bonesteel's proposal goes into the draft on the tenth of August. On the fifteenth, it is cabled to the Soviets. On the sixteenth, they say yes. Six days, from a map to a border.

talk.text: We felt it important to include the capital.
Soviet troops could enter the area before ours.

beats.say: The two men did not agree on everything, and they did not need to. Their task was small. It was not to decide the future of Korea. It was to choose a temporary line.
That is Rusk's own explanation, years later. The line was further north than American troops could realistically reach. He worried that the Soviets would get there first.
And here is a twist. Forty years earlier, Japan and Russia had discussed sharing Korea along the very same parallel. The two officers did not know.
The numbers were not equal. About sixteen million Koreans would live in the American zone, and nine million in the Soviet one.
Rusk later said something remarkable. If he had known Korean history, he would, quote, almost surely, have chosen a different line.
It was understood at the time that this was only temporary. A trusteeship would follow, and then independence. That is why almost nobody argued about the line at first.
But a line on paper is not yet a border. For that, someone has to say yes. And the person who had to say yes was in Moscow.
And that quick yes, as we will see, would be remembered in two different ways. In Washington, as relief. In Korea, as the moment the country was cut.
Dark humour writes itself here. A country that had lasted a thousand years was divided by two officers and a magazine map. But nobody on the ground was laughing.
Now the American plan had to survive one test. Would the Soviets accept the line? If they refused, they could simply keep marching south.
They said yes, immediately. To the surprise of the Americans, there was no argument.
In September, the Soviet administration issued its own currency. It was called the Red Army won. The north was already starting to run on its own rules.
The deal was written into General Order Number One, the surrender order for Japan. It was approved on the seventeenth of August.
Think about the timing. Within a week, a line chosen on short notice became a military order. Few people realised what it meant.
On the twenty-fourth of August, Soviet troops entered Pyongyang. They found a local committee for Korean independence already working, led by a veteran nationalist named Cho Man-sik.
Remember one thing. Japan did not simply leave. Its forces in the north destroyed factories, mines and official records. They gave the Soviets no help at all.
At first, the Soviets let such committees run. And most Koreans welcomed the Red Army, because it had fought Japan on Korean soil.

But the soldiers were poorly supplied. Some lacked shoes and uniforms. They lived off the land, and they looted. There were accusations of rape. These abuses faded when more disciplined units arrived.
The Soviet Union had been wrecked by the war. It lacked the money and the will to build a perfect satellite state. At the start, historians say, it had no firm plan for a permanent division.
The Soviets also brought Koreans who had lived in the Soviet Union, some of them members of its Communist Party. Their plan was to build a socialist state.
Meanwhile, in the south, nobody knew who was in charge. On the fifteenth of August, Japan announced its surrender. Koreans celebrated in Seoul.

In Seoul, the last Japanese governor-general, Nobuyuki Abe, tried to arrange a handover. He offered power to a respected newspaper man, Song Jin-woo. Song said no. He thought it would make him a puppet.
So Abe asked a different man. Lyuh Woon-hyung accepted. He formed a committee to prepare for independence, and it began to take over security in the city.
Around seven hundred and seventy-seven thousand Japanese lived in Korea, and they were horrified. Rumours flew. A Soviet army was coming by train. Some people panicked. Others celebrated.
On the sixteenth, young Japanese officers in Seoul protested their government's decisions, and warned they would punish any unrest. The city hung between joy and fear.
On the sixth of September, a congress in Seoul declared a People's Republic of Korea. It nominated Syngman Rhee, still in the United States, as its president.
The Americans never recognised it. On the seventh, General MacArthur issued Proclamation Number One. American military control, south of the thirty-eighth parallel.
General John Hodge landed at Incheon on the eighth. His troops were trained for fighting, not governing. And Washington had given him almost no guidance.
On the ninth, in the old throne room in Seoul, Japan's commanders signed the surrender. Hodge accepted it for the Allies. And the American occupation of southern Korea began.

The Japanese who lived in Korea were sent home. More than five hundred thousand left by December 1945, and nearly eight hundred thousand by the following August. They included almost all the industrial managers and technicians.

The south had been handed to John Hodge, an American general born in Illinois, who had fought in the First World War, and later at Guadalcanal. He knew how to command troops. Nobody had trained him to run a country.
But all of this was supposed to be temporary. And that is the question for the next chapter. What happened to the plan that was supposed to put Korea back together?
Prices rose sharply. The economy was disrupted. By the summer of 1946, the Americans introduced rationing and price controls. The south was free, but it was hungry.
Now the Soviets needed a Korean leader in the north. They found one in Kim Il Sung. Born Kim Song Ju in 1912, he had grown up in northeast China.
As a teenager, Kim became a communist. He fought in anti-Japanese guerrilla groups. In 1942, he joined the Soviet Red Army, and stayed in the Soviet Union until 1945.
The Soviets introduced him to the public in October 1945. In December, they chose him to lead the Communist Party in the north.
He spent the last years of the war training with Soviet troops in Manchuria. His supporters saw a war hero. His critics saw a Soviet creation. Historians still argue.
His strongest backer was a Soviet general, Terentii Shtykov. In 1946, Shtykov took charge of the administration, and pushed Moscow for money and support.
In March 1946, the northern government began a sweeping land reform. Land from Japanese owners and collaborators was divided among poor farmers. Many poor farmers gained land.
Major industries were nationalised. Yet the government was not purely Korean. Records say Soviet generals even designed the results of a 1946 election, down to the seats.
So in the north, Koreans gained land, jobs and pride. And they lost a free vote. Both of those things are true.
In February 1946, a provisional government began to rule the north. Within two years, it had become the machinery of a state.

Kim Il Sung would rule the north for more than forty-five years, until his death in 1994, and then his son would take over. But in 1945, he was a thirty-three-year-old whom most Koreans had not yet heard of.
Later, historians would say that Stalin himself and General Shtykov wrote the first constitution of 1948. The north was not a puppet, but it was not free either.
In the south, the loudest voice belonged to a man who had waited his whole life. Syngman Rhee was seventy years old.
Born in 1875, Rhee became a Christian and a young independence activist. He was jailed in 1899. After his release, he moved to the United States.
He rose in Korean politics fast. In 1919, he had been the first president of the Provisional Government in exile. In 1925, that government had impeached him.
There, he studied hard. He earned a degree from Harvard, and a doctorate from Princeton in 1910. He met two American presidents. And he lobbied for Korean independence for decades.
When he returned in 1945, he was a fierce anti-communist. And he wanted something very specific: a separate Korean state in the south, as soon as possible.
Rhee had a story that moved many Koreans. He had spent decades campaigning for Korean freedom. Later, in office, his rule would become authoritarian, and he would be forced to resign in 1960.
The Americans were not sure about him. But they needed a Korean they could work with. Rhee pressed Washington to give up on trusteeship and build a government in the south.
Meanwhile, the American occupation was chaotic. Historians contrast it with the calm occupation of Japan. Hodge reported to MacArthur in Tokyo, not to Washington.
Over the next few years, left-wing insurgents rose in the south, some backed by the north. Between thirty thousand and a hundred thousand people were killed. Most of them died on one island.
In 1945, Rhee and Kim had one thing in common. Neither had the power to draw the line. Both would try to use it.
Which brings us to the question the Americans and the Soviets now faced. Could two sides with opposite ideas build one country? And what would happen if they could not?

Prices soared. In September 1946, thousands of workers and peasants rose up against the military government. It was crushed. And Koreans in the south learned that independence would not be simple either.
What happened to the plan for trusteeship? In December 1945, foreign ministers met in Moscow. They agreed on a trusteeship over Korea of up to five years.
Four powers would share it: the United States, the Soviet Union, China and Britain. Then Korea would become independent.
Most Koreans were furious. They had just escaped thirty-five years of foreign rule. They wanted independence now.
Left and right split over it, and the split became deadly. The Korean Communist Party, close to Moscow, backed the trusteeship. Rhee's supporters fought it.
Look at one man caught inside that split. Cho Man-sik, in Pyongyang. Koreans called him the Gandhi of Korea, for his nonviolent resistance to Japan.
On the seventeenth of August 1945, at the Japanese governor's request, he formed a committee to keep order. The Soviets arrived, and hoped to win him over. He was the most popular leader in the city.
Then came the trusteeship. Cho thought it would bring in foreign influence, especially communist influence. On the first of January 1946, a Soviet officer asked him to sign his support. He refused.
Four days later, Soviet soldiers arrested him, and held him in a hotel in Pyongyang. He later disappeared into the prison system. He was probably shot in October 1950. Nobody has confirmed the date.
The man both Koreans and Soviets respected had no place in either future. The line left no room for the middle.
The Americans suspected a trap. The Soviets suspected one too. Every proposal, from either side, was judged by what the other side would gain from it.
A Soviet and American Joint Commission met in 1946 and 1947 to build a united government. It failed. It collapsed amid Cold War antagonism, and Korean opposition to the trusteeship.
The Soviets even proposed Lyuh Woon-hyung, the man who tried to bridge left and right. The Americans said no. In July 1947, Lyuh was assassinated by a nineteen-year-old.
Meanwhile, the border hardened. By May 1946, it was illegal to cross the thirty-eighth parallel without a permit. What had been a line on a map was now a border.
In September 1947, the Soviet delegate proposed that both armies simply leave, and let Koreans decide. The Americans refused. Here, both sides had a case, and both had fears.
So here is the pattern. Each side tried to unify Korea on its own terms. And each side's fear of the other made unity less likely.
And so, by early 1948, the choice was no longer between division and unity. It was between two kinds of division. One that Koreans might shape, and one that would be shaped for them.
This is where the plan failed. A temporary line needs a temporary arrangement. Without a deal in Moscow, the temporary line became something else.
The United States took the problem to the United Nations. In November 1947, the UN voted for free elections across Korea and for foreign troops to leave.
The Soviet Union boycotted the vote, and did not consider it binding. Without Soviet cooperation, the UN decided to hold elections only in the south.
Many Koreans understood at once what this meant. Separate elections would lead to separate countries. Strikes began in February 1948.
A United Nations commission was set up to watch the vote. Without Soviet cooperation, it could only work in the south.
In April, a rebellion erupted on Jeju, an island off the southern coast. Islanders opposed the division of the country. The government sent troops.

What followed was among the darkest episodes of this story. Estimates of the dead run from fourteen thousand to thirty thousand, around a tenth of the island's people. About half of Jeju's villages were burned.
Atrocities were committed by both sides. For decades, South Korea censored the story. We tell it plainly, and we leave a pause.

That same April, leaders from north and south met in Pyongyang and called for a united government. Rhee and Hodge denounced the meeting. One southern leader who attended, Kim Koo, was assassinated the next year.
In May, the south voted. In July, Rhee was elected president. On the fifteenth of August 1948, the Republic of Korea was born in the south.
Syngman Rhee became the first president of South Korea. He had been elected by the new assembly on the twentieth of July.
Twenty-five days later, on the ninth of September, the north proclaimed the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Kim Il Sung was its leader.
A line chosen on short notice was now two governments, two armies and two flags. Neither accepted the other as legitimate.
Both leaders now claimed to speak for all of Korea. Both said the other half was an illegitimate puppet. But only one of them was about to test that claim with an army.
Soviet troops left in December 1948. Two governments, each claiming the whole country, now faced each other across a line drawn on a magazine map.
From 1948, the armies of both sides fought bloody skirmishes along the border. Thousands died, years before the war officially began.
On the twenty-fifth of June 1950, North Korea invaded the south. Kim Il Sung had approved it, hoping to unify the country under communist rule.

The United Nations Security Council denounced the invasion. The Soviet representative was absent, so he could not veto it. Twenty-one countries joined the force, and the United States supplied about nine in ten of its soldiers.
Seoul fell in three days. As the army retreated, the south blew up the Han River bridge. About four thousand refugees were crossing it. Hundreds were killed.
The United Nations sent help, led by the United States. By August, the south held only a small corner around Busan.

Task Force Smith, the first American unit in action, was just five hundred and forty men. At Osan, on the fifth of July, they had no weapons that could stop the tanks. There were one hundred and eighty American casualties.
Then, on the fifteenth of September, UN forces landed at Incheon. They cut the enemy supply lines and took back Seoul. And the line did not stop them. They invaded the north.
Rhee argued that the northern attack had wiped out the border. MacArthur said he meant to unify Korea. They captured Pyongyang and moved on toward the Yalu River, the border with China.
On the nineteenth of October, Chinese troops crossed the Yalu. They pushed the UN forces back south. Seoul changed hands again.
By 1951, the front line settled near the thirty-eighth parallel again, almost exactly where it began. Then it became a war of attrition.

Both sides committed atrocities. The war's record includes mass killings of suspected communists by the South, a massacre at a hospital in Seoul by the North, and the heavy bombing of the North by the UN command.

In July 1951, armistice talks began. They dragged on for two years. Rhee demanded the war continue until Korea was unified under his leadership. The Communist side wanted an armistice line on the thirty-eighth parallel.

The UN side wanted a line based on the ground each side held, because it was easier to defend. In the end, that is what they got. The old parallel had been a map line. The new border was drawn by the fighting itself.
North Korea was bombed so heavily that almost all its major cities were destroyed. The war killed about a million soldiers and, by estimates, between one and a half and three million civilians.
The fighting ended on the twenty-seventh of July 1953. The Korean Armistice created a buffer zone four kilometres wide, the Demilitarized Zone.
Here is the strange part. The new border follows where the armies stood, not the old line. It crosses the thirty-eighth parallel at a diagonal.
Rhee refused to accept the armistice. Both Koreas wanted unity, each on its own terms. And no peace treaty has ever been signed.
Talks in 1954, in Geneva, failed to produce a united Korea. Since 1953, Swiss and Swedish soldiers have served on the commission that watches the armistice.
So who split Korea? The Americans would say they were in a hurry to stop a Soviet sweep. The Soviets would say they accepted a line, and did not plan a permanent wall.
Koreans would say it was never theirs to decide. They had waited thirty-five years for freedom, and then waited decades more for a country that was whole.
And historians keep arguing. Was the line chosen in a hurry, and then trapped by the Cold War? Or would the Cold War have found another line? Nobody can prove it.

So what became of the two men with the map? Start with Dean Rusk. In 1950, he became Assistant Secretary of State for Far Eastern Affairs. He played an influential part in America's decision to go to war in Korea.
Years later, he described the bombing of the North in a few flat words. The United States, he said, bombed everything that moved in North Korea, every brick standing on top of another.

card.text: Everything that moved in North Korea, every brick standing on top of another.

beats.say: In 1961, he became Secretary of State. He held the job for eight years, under Kennedy and Johnson.
Now Bonesteel. He became a general. And in 1966, he was sent to Korea, to command American forces there. Twenty-one years after he proposed the line, the man who drew it came back to guard it.

His years there were violent. North Korean infiltration, and clashes along the border. Historians call it the Korean DMZ Conflict. In January 1968, tensions rose again, with the Pueblo incident. He was photographed welcoming the crew of the Pueblo.

Bonesteel retired in 1969. He died in 1977, aged sixty-eight, and is buried at Arlington. Rusk died in 1994, aged eighty-five. That was the same year as Kim Il Sung. Neither man lived to see the line erased.
In 2018, the two leaders met at the border and signed the Panmunjom Declaration, which called for an end to hostile activities, and for reunification. The line is still there.

Today the Demilitarized Zone is about two hundred and fifty kilometres long, and four wide. Between 1953 and 1999, violence along it killed more than five hundred South Korean soldiers, about fifty Americans, and about two hundred and fifty North Koreans. Yet it holds.

And here is the strangest twist. With people kept out for decades, the zone became a refuge for wildlife. More than a hundred of Korea's two hundred and sixty-seven endangered animals live there, among them the red-crowned crane.
One line, drawn on a map by two tired officers. Their zone was meant to be temporary. It has now lasted more than eighty years.
Rusk said he would almost surely have chosen another line, if he had known Korea's history. The people who had to live with it never got to choose at all.

outro.text: Every border has two sides. This one was drawn by two young officers, accepted by a dictator, and lived with by millions.
outro.question: Was the 38th parallel an accident of a hurried night, or was the Cold War always going to split Korea?

hook: In August 1945, two young American officers were handed a magazine map and almost no time. They cut Korea in half.
about: How the 38th parallel split Korea, told from both sides: Japan's rule and the Cairo promise, the Soviet entry on 10 August 1945, Dean Rusk and Charles Bonesteel and a National Geographic map, Stalin's quick yes, Hodge and Kim Il Sung, Syngman Rhee's return, the failed trusteeship, the UN elections, Jeju, the two republics of 1948, the Korean War, and the armistice of 1953.

de.title: Wie zwei Männer und eine Karte Korea teilten: Der 38. Breitengrad von beiden Seiten
de.description:
Im August 1945 bekamen zwei junge amerikanische Offiziere eine Magazinkarte und fast keine Zeit. Sie teilten Korea in zwei Hälften.

Die Teilung Koreas, erzählt von beiden Seiten: Japans Herrschaft, das Versprechen von Kairo, der Einmarsch der Sowjets, Rusk und Bonesteel, Stalins schnelles Ja, Hodge und Kim Il Sung, Syngman Rhees Rückkehr, die gescheiterte Treuhandschaft, die UN-Wahlen, Jeju, die zwei Republiken von 1948, der Koreakrieg und der Waffenstillstand von 1953.

es.title: Cómo dos hombres y un mapa dividieron Corea: el paralelo 38 desde ambos lados
es.description:
En agosto de 1945, dos jóvenes oficiales estadounidenses recibieron un mapa de revista y casi nada de tiempo. Cortaron Corea por la mitad.

La división de Corea contada desde ambos lados: el dominio japonés, la promesa de El Cairo, la entrada soviética, Rusk y Bonesteel, el rápido sí de Stalin, Hodge y Kim Il Sung, el regreso de Syngman Rhee, la tutela fallida, las elecciones de la ONU, Jeju, las dos repúblicas de 1948, la guerra de Corea y el armisticio de 1953.

fr.title: Comment deux hommes et une carte ont divisé la Corée : le 38e parallèle des deux côtés
fr.description:
En août 1945, deux jeunes officiers américains reçoivent une carte de magazine et presque aucun temps. Ils coupent la Corée en deux.

La division de la Corée racontée des deux côtés : la domination japonaise, la promesse du Caire, l'entrée des Soviétiques, Rusk et Bonesteel, le oui rapide de Staline, Hodge et Kim Il Sung, le retour de Syngman Rhee, la tutelle ratée, les élections de l'ONU, Jeju, les deux républiques de 1948, la guerre de Corée et l'armistice de 1953.

pt.title: Como dois homens e um mapa dividiram a Coreia: o paralelo 38 dos dois lados
pt.description:
Em agosto de 1945, dois jovens oficiais americanos receberam um mapa de revista e quase nenhum tempo. Eles cortaram a Coreia ao meio.

A divisão da Coreia contada dos dois lados: o domínio japonês, a promessa do Cairo, a entrada soviética, Rusk e Bonesteel, o sim rápido de Stálin, Hodge e Kim Il Sung, a volta de Syngman Rhee, a tutela fracassada, as eleições da ONU, Jeju, as duas repúblicas de 1948, a Guerra da Coreia e o armistício de 1953.
